reading_plan: Source title: Sustainable AI infrastructure: A scenario-based forecast of water footprint under uncertainty. Source type: peer_reviewed_paper. First look: a 12-page, two-column Journal of Cleaner Production research article, with front-matter highlights and abstract, a literature-rich technical narrative, displayed equations, cooling schematics, a map, forecast and sensitivity plots, three tables, an algorithm, disclosures, an Appendix, and about two pages of references. The prose is moderately dense, becoming more technical in the accounting and probabilistic-method sections. I will follow natural paragraph and subsection breaks, generally taking roughly 200–500 source words per step and slowing down for definitions, assumptions, equations, and numerical results. I read extracted PDFKit text alongside rendered page images; readings of visual elements are paraphrases, with no inferred precise chart values. Repeated claims will be noted as restatements in their later setting.

reading_path.location: p. 1, Highlights and Abstract
reading_path.moves: Announces the problem, defines the three-part scope, previews a probabilistic method and its findings, and frames the study around mitigation and planning. The opening adopts a sustainability perspective in which overlooked water demand deserves attention alongside energy.

claims.text: Rapid AI and cloud expansion is creating a significant, often overlooked impact on global water resources.
The assessment distinguishes on-site operational consumption, off-site electricity-generation consumption, and embodied consumption in hardware and supply chains.
A Bayesian-inspired scenario-based probabilistic framework combines sparse empirical data, expert-informed assumptions, and policy-relevant trajectories to forecast 2030 and 2050 demand.
Without mitigation, global data-centre water consumption could increase more than seven times by mid-century, with cooling-related operational consumption accounting for most demand.

Cooling efficiency, alternative technologies, electricity sourcing, and siting that considers regional water availability are mitigation levers; sensitivity analysis highlights compute growth and efficiency trends.
The framework offers a transparent, adaptable basis for aligning AI infrastructure development with long-term water sustainability goals.

reading_path.meaning: The opening supplies the authors’ stated purpose and preview. These are introductory claims, whose development remains ahead; the journey begins with water sustainability as the organising concern.

claims.text: Algorithm 1 loops through each scenario and year from 2025 to 2050, samples baseline server energy, and compounds it by the scenario growth rate.
Algorithm 1 compounds WUE, PUE, and EWIF downward by their annual improvement rates; embodied water is its baseline multiplied by the compounded EWU improvement and divided by equipment lifespan T0.
Algorithm 1 multiplies energy by WUE for on-site water and by PUE and EWIF for off-site water, divides the operational sum and embodied amount by 10^9, then stores simulated means and intervals.
Spatially disaggregated modelling could use location-specific efficiency parameters, but is outside the present scope.

The framework is designed for scheduled reassessment: inputs such as WUE, PUE, and EWIF could be updated annually or biannually and simulations rerun to improve tracking, policy, and investment decisions.

reading_path.meaning: The algorithm makes the compounding and aggregation rules explicit. The updating proposal is a prospective use of the framework, and the spatial extension is deliberately reserved rather than treated as part of the current implementation.

reading_path.moves: States methodological strengths, explains data scarcity, concedes simplifying assumptions, and proposes extensions.

claims.text: The approach is well suited to scarce or fast-changing data because it combines expert judgement and scenario assumptions transparently and can forecast without comprehensive historical datasets.
Commercial sensitivities and cybersecurity concerns lead many companies not to disclose detailed water-use statistics, obstructing traditional modelling.
Although variables interact in deterministic equations, probabilistic inputs are treated independently, with no modelled statistical dependencies or correlations.
This simplification may overlook important interrelationships during simultaneous policy or technology changes; disruption and regional feedback may produce nonlinear effects.
Future models should incorporate these effects; real-time monitoring and a dynamic Bayesian framework are promising directions for greater accuracy.

reading_path.meaning: This section qualifies the method’s adaptability with a concrete independence assumption. The concession does not retract the scenario results, but specifies relationships the current model leaves unrepresented.

claims.text: Real-time AI-driven cooling optimisation should be promoted.
Sustainability reporting should require disclosure of WUE, EWIF, and EWU.

support.text: The disclosure recommendation cites the World Water Development Report.

claims.text: Siting decisions should incorporate water availability to avoid clustering in already stressed areas.

reading_path.meaning: The recommendations follow the earlier three-component accounting and cooling comparisons. They combine technical choices, supply-chain accounting, disclosure, and siting, extending beyond the parameters directly varied in the forecasts.

reading_path.location: p. 9, Section 6.3 end, waste heat and geographic refinement
reading_path.moves: Identifies an unmodelled opportunity, returns to the geographical mismatch, and recommends a regionalised extension. The recommendation to incorporate climate and water-stress indicators into siting is repeated.

claims.text: Reuse of computing waste heat for residential or district heating may indirectly reduce energy and water consumption; it was not explicitly modelled and should be evaluated alongside cooling and siting measures.
Many fast-growing clusters are located in water-stressed areas because low electricity prices, renewables, tax incentives, and land availability take priority over hydrological suitability.

Although global in scope, the framework can be adapted to location-specific climate classifications, WUE benchmarks, and energy-water interactions to align digital growth with sustainability and avoid freshwater conflicts.

reading_path.meaning: This passage restates the siting concern with a clearer account of economic incentives and identifies how future modelling could address it. Waste-heat reuse remains explicitly outside the present simulation.

reading_path.location: pp. 9–10, Section 7, summary and future research
reading_path.moves: Restates contributions and principal results, characterises the contribution positively, and proposes specific modelling extensions. The conclusion restates the framework’s novelty, its claimed significance and flexibility under data scarcity, the cooling and compute-growth levers, the unchecked-growth warning, and the cooling, alternative-water, and siting responses.

claims.text: Regional disaggregation could sum consumption across regions with location-specific WUE, EWIF, and embodied intensity, better representing uneven infrastructure and environmental pressures.
Future regional models should reflect differences in climate, infrastructure, electricity mix, regulation, facility density, cooling adoption, and local water stress.
Dynamic Bayesian modelling could integrate real-time data; a unified water-energy-emissions metric would offer a more comprehensive environmental assessment.

reading_path.meaning: The conclusion recapitulates rather than introduces another set of model outputs. Its forward-looking contribution is the proposed regional summation and richer sustainability assessment; the claim of significance is the authors’ own evaluative framing.

reading_path.location: p. 10, Section 7 end and authorship/interest statements
reading_path.moves: Ends with a conditional mitigation claim and coordinated-action agenda, then gives responsibility and competing-interest disclosures. The closing action agenda repeats accelerated immersion/closed-loop cooling, standardised operational and embodied accounting, climate-aware siting, and greater real-time disclosure, and adds funding water-efficient hardware and systems RD&D.

claims.text: Strategic improvements in WUE, EWIF, and hardware life-cycle management could reduce 2050 water use by up to 95% relative to BAU.
Industry, regulators, and researchers should jointly fund research, development, and demonstration of water-efficient AI hardware and systems.

The CRediT statement assigns Herrera conception, data curation, formal analysis, investigation, methodology, software, validation, visualisation, and drafting/revision; the coauthors share investigation, methodology, supervision, validation, analysis, visualisation, and writing roles in different combinations.
The authors declare no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work.

reading_path.meaning: The authors close with the possibility of a much lower-water future and an action agenda, then shift to disclosures. The 95% figure is preserved as a conditional claim relative to BAU, without substituting an unstated baseline or mechanism.

reading_path.location: p. 10, Appendix, sensitivity design, Fig. A.7, and Table A.3
reading_path.moves: Reports a parameter-perturbation exercise, ranks leverage, translates relative effects to absolute volumes, and reinforces the mitigation interpretation.

claims.text: The sensitivity analysis varies WUE, PUE, EWIF, and EWU by ±20% for 2050 under BAU.

Figure A.7 shows negative and positive parameter-change bars around zero; WUE has the widest responses, EWIF and PUE follow, and the embodied row is shortest. The embodied row is labelled EWE in the plot. Exact bar endpoints are not numerically labelled, so no precise values are estimated from their lengths.

Table A.3 gives a BAU baseline of 28.11 billion litres/day; WUE has a 16.7% relative difference and 4.69 billion litres/day absolute difference, PUE 14.3% and 4.02, EWIF 15.1% and 4.24, and EWU 4.6% and 1.29.

Under the stated baseline, a 20% WUE improvement reduces demand by 4.69 billion litres/day and deterioration increases it by a similar amount; comparable absolute differences are 4.24 for EWIF, 4.02 for PUE, and 1.29 for EWU.

support.text: The Appendix prose states these absolute effects and refers to Table A.3.

claims.text: Cooling and power infrastructure improvements have the greatest potential to reduce long-term demand; hardware design and procurement also matter and should not be overlooked.

support.text: The authors draw this conclusion from the sensitivity ranking and the smaller but nonzero embodied contribution.

reading_path.meaning: The Appendix supplies the sensitivity evidence repeatedly invoked in the discussion. Plot and table readings are recorded separately, preserving the printed table values and avoiding an inferred reconciliation of the chart’s bar lengths with those values.
